text: The core limitation of every large language model is the same. It was trained on data up to a cutoff date and it has no access to your specific data. RAG solves both problems simultaneously. Understanding exactly how it solves them and where it can fail is what separates AI engineers from AI users. In this lesson, RAG retrieval augmented generation is an architecture that combines a retrieval system. Finds relevant information from a knowledge base with a generation system, the LLM that produces the final response. The basic flow user asks the question arrow retriever finds relevant documents. Arrow documents are added to the LLM context, window arrow LLM generates a response grounded in retrieved documents. The retrieval step uses vector embeddings. Every document in your knowledge base is converted into a vector, a list of numbers that represents its meaning in high-dimensional space. When a user asks a question, the question is also converted into a vector. The retriever finds documents whose vectors are nearest to the question vector. nearest vectors equals similar meaning. This is semantic search. Finding documents that mean the same thing as the question, not just documents that contain the same words. The embedding model converts text to vectors, common choices, open AI text dash embedding dash 3, dash small, high quality paid API, sentence transformers, all dash mini LM dash L6 dash V2 free runs locally good for English, paraphrase dash multilingual dash mini LM dash L12 dash V2 free supports Wahili and other African languages. The vector database stores embeddings and enables fast similarity search, common choices, pine cone, managed cloud, scales to billions of vectors, chroma, local development, open source, super base, PG vector, postgres extension, excellent for production apps that already use super base. The critical design decisions, chunk size, how large are the document segments you embed, chunk overlap, do chunk share content at boundaries, top k retrieval, how many chunks do you retrieve per query and re-ranking, do you apply a second pass model to reorder retrieved chunks by relevance. Each decision affects answer quality and latency, where r a g fails, one retrieval failure. The right document exists but is not retrieved because the query and document use different words for the same concept. Two, context window overflow, too many retrieved chunks push important content out of the LLM context. Three, hallucination on retrieved content, the LLM generates plausible sounding content that slightly misrepresent the retrieved documents. Four, stale data, the knowledge base is not updated frequently enough. Five, language mismatch, African language documents embedded with English optimized models produce poor retrieval quality. The quality of a r a g system is determined by two independent failure modes, retrieval failure, finding the wrong documents, and generation failure, misrepresenting the right documents. You can have perfect retrieval and terrible generation, or perfect generation on terrible retrieved documents. Debugging requires isolating which component is failing. Vocabulary, mismatch between user queries and document language is the most common retrieval failure in real world r a g systems. Hybrid retrieval, semantic plus keyword, handles it better than pure vector search alone. Always test your retrieval with queries that use different words from those in your source documents. Remember this, test r a g retrieval before testing r a g generation. If you cannot confirm that the right documents are being retrieved for your test queries, you are debugging the wrong component. Apply what you learn in this lesson, and you will see results immediately. Your skills bear fruit.
